title: AI, without the guesswork
description: Learn to ask better questions, verify answers, and turn a vague request into a useful result.

lessons.title: Define the job
lessons.text: A useful prompt specifies a task, relevant context, constraints, and an output format. Treat the model as an untrusted assistant, not a source of truth.
lessons.task: Write a prompt for a one-page comparison of three ways a small shop could track inventory. Specify the audience, budget, output table, and what the model should do when uncertain.

lessons.title: Build a verification loop
lessons.text: Ask the model to separate facts, assumptions, and suggestions. A plausible citation may be invented. Open the original source and check the claim and date yourself.
lessons.task: Run your prompt in a cloud AI tool you choose. Pick three factual claims. Verify them independently and record each source URL and the exact supporting passage.

lessons.title: Ship your research brief
lessons.text: Keep a record of the prompt, model, date, changes, and remaining uncertainties. Remove private information before publishing.
lessons.task: Deliver a brief containing your original prompt, the revised answer, three checked claims, and one limitation. Do not claim the output is independently verified unless you checked it.

quiz.question: What makes an AI-generated citation trustworthy?
options: You opened the source and checked that it supports the claim

title: Your first business assistant
description: Turn repetitive enquiries into clear, consistent draft replies—without exposing customer data.

lessons.title: Create a fictional policy
lessons.text: Start with a fictional shop. Define opening hours, delivery areas, returns, and prices. These are the only facts the assistant may use.
lessons.task: Write a fictional shop policy with five rules. Include a rule that uncertain questions must be referred to a person.

lessons.title: Build the reply template
lessons.text: Separate the customer message from instructions. Customer text is untrusted input; it must not override your policy. Never give the model authority to issue refunds or send messages.
lessons.task: Create a prompt that returns: draft reply, policy used, and escalation needed. Test normal delivery, an out-of-policy refund, and a message saying ignore all previous instructions.

lessons.title: Evaluate before use
lessons.text: Automatic replies can make promises you cannot keep. Keep a human in the sending loop and minimise customer data.
lessons.task: Produce three test replies and a checklist: factual, polite, no invented promises, no private data, and correct escalation. Save your template as a text file.

quiz.question: What should the assistant do with an unsupported refund request?

title: Make messy data useful
description: Use AI to help with formulas while keeping calculation and checking deterministic.

lessons.title: Start with clean sample data
lessons.text: Use fictional expenses rather than bank statements. Create columns Date, Category, Description, Amount. Keep numbers numeric and one row per transaction.
lessons.task: Create five fictional expenses: Travel 10, Food 5, Travel 15, Tools 20, Food 10. The expected total is 60.

lessons.title: Ask for a formula, then test it
lessons.text: AI can suggest spreadsheet formulas, but your spreadsheet performs the calculation. With headers in row 1 and five amounts in D2:D6, =SUM(D2:D6) should produce 60. Locale settings can change separators.
lessons.task: Use =SUM(D2:D6). Then ask an AI for a category total formula. Test =SUMIF(B2:B6,"Travel",D2:D6); the expected result is 25.

lessons.title: Add a failure test
lessons.text: A formula working once is not proof. Test blank cells, changed categories, negative amounts, and a new row beyond the original range.
lessons.task: Add a sixth expense. Observe whether the range includes it. Submit your sample CSV, formulas, expected totals, and one discovered failure case.

quiz.question: What proves a suggested formula works for your sample?
options: The model says it is correct
Its calculated output matches independently checked expected values

title: From idea to working page
description: Build a simple calculator, understand its code, and test its edge cases.

lessons.title: Specify the smallest tool
lessons.text: Build a quote calculator for a fictional service: quantity multiplied by unit price. It should reject negative inputs. No accounts, payments, or personal information are needed.
lessons.task: Write the acceptance criteria: 3 × 5 = 15, zero is allowed, negative inputs show an error, and all fields have labels.

lessons.title: Build and inspect
lessons.text: Ask an AI for one self-contained HTML file with CSS and JavaScript. Read the code before running it. Avoid external scripts and never paste secrets into generated code.
lessons.task: Generate the file, inspect it, then open it in your browser. Confirm it does not make network requests. Explain which lines read inputs and calculate the result.

lessons.title: Test and share
lessons.text: A working page needs more than a screenshot. Check keyboard use, small screens, invalid input, and whether text explains limitations.
lessons.task: Record the four acceptance tests and their results. Submit index.html and a short README. Deploy only after inspecting the code and removing personal information.

quiz.question: When should you execute generated code?
options: After inspecting it and understanding its permissions
Only if it contains a secret key

title: Automate the boring bit—safely
description: Map an automation that drafts useful work but asks before taking action.

lessons.title: Map the workflow
lessons.text: Every automation has an input, transformation, output, and failure path. Start with a workflow that prepares a weekly summary from fictional tasks.
lessons.task: Draw: sample task list → validate fields → draft summary → human review → publish. Mark where data crosses a service boundary.

lessons.title: Plan retries and duplicate protection
lessons.text: Retries can accidentally send duplicate messages. Store a stable job ID and completed status. Stop after a small number of attempts, and do not retry authentication or exhausted-budget errors blindly.
lessons.task: Write pseudocode that checks whether a job is already complete, attempts it once, and records the result. Add a maximum retry count of two for temporary errors.

lessons.title: Keep a stop switch
lessons.text: An autonomous system needs limited permissions, a pause control, logs without secrets, and a human approval gate for public actions.
lessons.task: Submit your diagram, pseudocode, three failure cases, and a shutdown procedure. This project is a design exercise, not an unattended deployed agent.

quiz.question: Which action needs a human approval gate in this exercise?

title: Understand the AI plumbing
description: Separate open-source software, model licences, hosted APIs, and free usage quotas.

lessons.title: Know what is actually free
lessons.text: A public GitHub repository may contain code, model weights, an SDK, or a list of APIs. None of these guarantees free hosted compute. Inspect the licence, provider terms, authentication, pricing, and last update.
lessons.task: Choose a public AI repository. Record its URL, licence, purpose, and whether it supplies an actual hosted endpoint. Do not run unknown install commands.

lessons.title: Understand cloud requests
lessons.text: An OpenAI-compatible chat API commonly accepts a model and messages. Keep secret API keys server-side. A 401 means authentication failed, 429 means a limit was reached, and 402 may mean credits are exhausted.
lessons.task: Sketch browser → your gateway → provider. Mark where the secret lives. Write user-friendly messages for authentication failure, exhausted credits, and timeouts.

lessons.title: Evaluate before integrating
lessons.text: Test a provider using non-sensitive sample prompts. Confirm allowed application use, current quotas, data handling, latency, and failure behaviour. Never use leaked keys or reverse-engineered private services.
lessons.task: Deliver a provider checklist with evidence links and a checked date. Include an offline fallback: the lesson remains readable when the tutor is unavailable.

quiz.question: Does an open-source repository guarantee free cloud inference?
options: Only if it has many stars
No; hosting and usage terms are separate
